strengths: Novel formulation of deformable image registration as latent-space policy optimization via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), successfully avoiding the intractability of high-dimensional RL over dense 3D deformation vector fields.

The introduction of Latent-Dimension Variance Normalization (LDVN) is mathematically simple yet effective, addressing the variance explosion in log-likelihood calculations when dealing with tens of thousands of latent dimensions in dense vision tasks.

Thorough evaluation across three diverse 3D datasets (OASIS brain MRI, LiTS liver CT, and cross-modality Abdomen MR-CT) and three distinct backbones (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans), demonstrating consistent gains in Dice score and reductions in folding (NJD).
Detailed ablation studies that isolate the impact of the unsupervised warm-up, number of rollout trajectories and refinement steps, and demonstrate notable label efficiency under scarce supervision.
weaknesses: The test-time inference procedure needs clearer specification. During training (Algorithm 1 and Eq. 17), the trajectory is updated using the best trajectory $j^* = \arg\max_j R^{(j)}$, which depends on ground-truth segmentation masks. At test time, ground truth labels are unavailable; the paper should explicitly explain whether inference deterministically sets $z = \mu$ with $\tau=0$ across $T$ recurrent steps, or whether an unsupervised image-similarity metric is used to rank trajectories.

Theoretical connection of LDVN to policy gradient scaling: Dividing the log-likelihood by $s \propto \sqrt{N}$ in Eq. (12) essentially rescales the policy gradient magnitude by $1/s$. The manuscript would benefit from a deeper discussion contrasting LDVN against standard gradient clipping or temperature annealing/entropy regularization.

While Table 3 compares '+ Multi-step' against '+ GRPO', the exact architectural and training difference between row 4 and standard iterative/recurrent registration baselines (e.g., standard cascades like Recursive Cascaded Networks or LapIRN) could be articulated more directly to further demarcate the precise RL-driven benefits.

strengths: Novel and elegant formulation: The paper bridges the gap between reinforcement learning and 3D deformable image registration (DIR) by cleverly defining the policy distribution over high-resolution latent representations at the encoder bottleneck, bypassing the intractability of million-dimensional deformation fields without collapsing to overly restrictive rigid/low-dimensional parameterizations.

Theoretical and practical contribution in LDVN: The proposed Latent-Dimension Variance Normalization (LDVN) effectively addresses the variance explosion problem inherent when computing Gaussian log-likelihoods over tens of thousands of latent dimensions, providing unbiased scaling that stabilizes GRPO in high-dimensional dense vision settings.

Effective label efficiency framework: Combining unsupervised warm-up with multi-trajectory weakly supervised GRPO allows models to iteratively reuse scarce segmentation annotations, demonstrating remarkable gains in data efficiency (e.g., reaching 98.5% of full-label performance with only 60% labeled samples).

Comprehensive empirical validation: MorphSeek is evaluated across three diverse benchmarks (intra-modality brain MRI, abdominal CT, and challenging cross-modality MR-CT) and three representative architectures (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans), consistently achieving statistically significant improvements in Dice overlap while simultaneously reducing folding artifacts (NJD).

Insightful ablations: The paper provides thorough ablation experiments covering the number of trajectories, refinement steps, label scaling behavior, necessity of unsupervised warm-up, and runtime/parameter overhead.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding test-time inference: While Algorithm 1 details the training procedure—where the best trajectory $j^*$ is greedily selected using reward calculated from ground truth segmentation masks $S_f, S_m$—the exact inference pipeline is not clearly described in Section 3. At test time, ground truth masks are unavailable; the paper should explicitly state whether inference runs deterministically ($z = \mu$, $\tau = 0$) recursively over $T$ steps, or if another mechanism is used.

Evaluation metric diversity: The quantitative evaluation is limited strictly to Dice and NJD (%). Standard surface distance metrics widely adopted in registration benchmarks (such as 95% Hausdorff Distance [HD95] and Average Symmetric Surface Distance [ASSD]) are missing from the main results, which would provide a more complete assessment of boundary alignment quality.

Training memory footprint and scalability: As shown in Table 2, scaling to 8 trajectories leads to out-of-memory (OOM) errors even with batch size 1, since multiple full 3D intermediate feature graphs and warpings must be maintained. A clearer discussion of the GPU memory requirements during training compared to standard end-to-end training would enhance practical reproducibility and adoption.

strengths: Novel paradigm adapting Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to 3D deformable image registration by casting the action space into the latent bottleneck of an encoder-decoder architecture rather than unmanageable dense 3D displacement fields or overly compressed 1D vectors.

Introduction of Latent-Dimension Variance Normalization (LDVN), addressing the severe gradient variance and log-likelihood explosion inherent to tens of thousands of latent dimensions in 3D dense feature representations.

Consistent empirical improvements across multiple backbones (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans) and diverse datasets (OASIS brain MRI, LiTS liver CT, and cross-modality Abdomen MR-CT), demonstrating gains in overlap (Dice) alongside reductions in non-diffeomorphic foldings (NJD).
Detailed ablation studies examining the effect of trajectory sampling count, refinement steps, label efficiency under small sample regimes, and the necessity of unsupervised warm-up.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding the exact test-time inference protocol: In Algorithm 1 and Eq. 17, the training step greedily selects the best trajectory $j^*$ based on ground-truth segmentation masks ($S_m, S_f$). At test time, ground-truth masks are unavailable. While Table 4 reports 1/2/3-step test latencies, the manuscript does not formally define how multi-step inference operates without labels (e.g., whether it runs deterministically with $\tau=0$ and $z=\mu$ in a recurrent loop).

Incomplete registration metrics: Deformable image registration benchmarks typically require complementary boundary distance metrics such as the 95% Hausdorff Distance (HD95) or Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD) to verify boundary fidelity alongside volumetric Dice and Jacobian determinants (|J| < 0).

Conceptual tension with differentiable relaxations: The framework retains a supervised differentiable soft-Dice loss ($L_{\text{Dice}}$) directly backpropagating gradients through the network alongside the RL policy loss ($L_{\text{policy}}$). The specific mechanism by which the non-differentiable reward optimization provides advantages over existing end-to-end differentiable recurrent/cascaded registration models needs deeper theoretical or empirical isolation.

Missing self-contained proofs: Critical derivations referenced in Section 3.3 regarding the asymptotic variance scaling of the summation terms $X_i$ and the choice of $s \propto \sqrt{N}$ are deferred to the Appendix, which was not included with the main submission.

strengths: Novel formulation of deformable image registration as latent-space policy optimization: By parameterizing the policy over the encoder bottleneck features rather than either ultra-low-dimensional global vectors (which lose fine spatial detail) or full voxel-wise displacement fields (which are computationally intractable for RL), MorphSeek finds an effective middle ground for RL in dense visual alignment.

Principled and well-analyzed normalization scheme (LDVN): The paper identifies that high-dimensional latent spaces ($N \approx 10^5$) cause extreme variance in GRPO log-likelihoods and formally derives the $s \propto \sqrt{N}$ variance scaling factor. Proposition 1 demonstrates that affine transformations with zero-mean advantages preserve policy-gradient directions.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: The method is validated across three diverse 3D datasets (monomodal brain MRI, liver CT, and challenging cross-modality abdomen MR–CT) across three representative backbone architectures (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, and NICE-Trans), demonstrating statistically significant gains in both Dice overlap and topological regularity (NJD).

Thorough ablations and diagnostic studies: The submission provides exhaustive ablation studies on trajectory count, refinement steps, label efficiency (demonstrating high performance with very few labeled pairs), posterior collapse, and hyperparameter sensitivity, as well as a well-reasoned discussion on why baseline methods like SPAC cannot reliably report cumulative NJD.
weaknesses: High training memory footprint: Because GRPO samples $J$ trajectories per step in a 3D dense feature space, memory scaling is severe; as reported in Table 2, scaling beyond 6 trajectories triggers out-of-memory errors even on 80GB A800 GPUs, which limits accessibility and democratization.

Inference latency overhead: The multi-step coarse-to-fine refinement scales inference time roughly linearly with step count $T$ (e.g., TransMorph inference increases from 401 ms to 1,376 ms for 3 steps, and VoxelMorph-L reaches ~2,022 ms), trading runtime efficiency for registration accuracy compared to pure single-shot feedforward approaches.

Small test cohorts on select tasks: The Abdomen MR–CT task evaluates on only 8 official paired scans and LiTS on 40 test pairs. While standard in the Learn2Reg benchmark context, evaluating on larger clinical cohorts would further strengthen the empirical reliability of the conclusions.

strengths: Original and well-motivated framework: Reformulating deformable image registration as multi-trajectory, multi-step policy optimization in the encoder's high-dimensional latent space effectively bridges the gap between low-dimensional RL registration (e.g., rigid or heavily compressed latents like SPAC) and dense 3D deformation fields.

Solid theoretical and empirical justification for LDVN: The authors provide a clear mathematical rationale showing that scaling the group-relative log-likelihood by s proportional to sqrt(N) controls gradient variance in high-dimensional latent spaces while preserving the exact policy gradient direction, supported by Monte Carlo verification and ablation experiments.

Comprehensive empirical validation: MorphSeek demonstrates consistent and statistically significant gains in Dice overlap while reducing folding artifacts (NJD) across three distinct benchmarks (OASIS brain MRI, LiTS liver CT, and cross-modal Abdomen MR-CT) and three representative architectures (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, and NICE-Trans).

High label efficiency: The multi-trajectory exploration allows the framework to extract substantial supervisory signals from limited labeled pairs, approaching full-label accuracy with only a fraction of annotated data.

Thorough ablations and insightful analysis: The manuscript and supplementary material provide detailed examinations of posterior collapse, the necessity of the warm-up prior to avoid reward hacking, hyperparameter sensitivity, and a clear explanation of why previous multi-step methods like SPAC struggle with reliable Jacobian determinant evaluation.
weaknesses: Multi-step inference latency overhead: Although the parameter overhead is minimal (<3%), multi-step evaluation naturally multiplies inference latency (e.g., increasing TransMorph runtime from ~401 ms to ~1376 ms for T=3 steps), which may impact time-sensitive or real-time clinical workflows.

Sensitivity and complexity of the training pipeline: The overall training procedure combines unsupervised warm-up, KL divergence schedules, multi-trajectory sampling, LDVN, reward weights (wDice, wNJD), temperature annealing, and auxiliary losses (Lwarm, LDice). As demonstrated in Table 5, the optimization can be sensitive to hyperparameter deviations (e.g., yielding exploration collapse or instability).

Limited evaluation metrics: The evaluation focuses primarily on Dice overlap and NJD. Reporting additional clinically relevant registration metrics, such as Target Registration Error (TRE) on anatomical landmarks or surface distance metrics (e.g., 95% Hausdorff Distance) where available (such as in Learn2Reg tasks), would further substantiate geometric alignment quality.

strengths: Novel and elegant problem formulation: Reformulating deformable image registration as latent-space policy optimization effectively overcomes the dimensional curse that previously restricted RL-based medical registration to rigid transformations or extreme low-dimensional latent bottlenecks.

Sound theoretical motivation and stabilization: The proposed Latent-Dimension Variance Normalization (LDVN) provides a mathematically principled scaling ($s \propto \sqrt{N}$) to control the variance of log-likelihoods in high-dimensional Gaussian policies, with a formal proof that gradient directions are preserved under zero-mean advantages.

Consistent empirical gains across architectures and tasks: Evaluated across three 3D registration benchmarks (OASIS brain MRI, LiTS CT, Abdomen MR-CT) and three distinct backbones (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans), MorphSeek achieves consistent and statistically significant Dice improvements while maintaining lower negative Jacobian determinant (NJD) rates.

High label efficiency: The multi-trajectory exploration effectively re-samples and reuses scarce segmentation annotations across refinement steps, demonstrating that ~98.5% of full-supervision accuracy can be reached with only 60% labeled data.

Comprehensive supplementary material: The appendix provides extensive ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, posterior-collapse verification, classical baseline comparisons (SyN, deedsBCV), and a clear analysis of why post-hoc composition in previous RL baselines (like SPAC) prevents reliable NJD evaluation.
weaknesses: Unclear test-time multi-step inference procedure: While Section 3.3 and Algorithm 1 detail how ground-truth segmentation masks are used to greedily select the highest-reward trajectory ($j^* = \arg\max R^{(j)}$) during training, the main text lacks explicit detail on how trajectory selection or multi-step propagation is performed at test time when annotations are unavailable (e.g., whether it uses deterministic mean $\mu$ with re-encoding, or unsupervised similarity metrics).

High training resource footprint: Sampling $J=6$ latent trajectories across $T=3$ steps per volume requires substantial VRAM and computational time. The paper notes that $J=8$ leads to out-of-memory errors on 80GB A800 GPUs with batch size 1. A more explicit discussion on training wall-clock time compared to standard supervised/unsupervised training would help assess practical adoptability.

Evaluation metrics could be broadened: While Dice and NJD are standard, medical image registration benchmarks (such as Learn2Reg) typically also assess landmark alignment via Target Registration Error (TRE) or boundary distance via 95% Hausdorff Distance (HD95) to ensure that improvements in overlap translate to genuine anatomical landmark accuracy.
